title: The Oldest Manuscript of The Song of Roland Is Actually an English Performer's Copy
dek: The Oxford Digby 23 manuscript is written in Anglo-Norman, and scholars date it to between 1140 and 1170 by the degree of dialect drift — the most complete version of this French epic was performed for the English.
why: This is a members-only sample episode, medium information density, but it gets very concrete about how a manuscript gets read as "some minstrel's working copy" — good for listeners interested in manuscripts, oral epic and dialect reconstruction.
who: Listeners interested in medieval manuscripts, oral epic and dialect reconstruction; anyone who wants to see how a single manuscript gets reconstructed into a specific performance setting.
skip: If you only want the political subtext of The Song of Roland, you can skip it — that part is in the next episode.

points.h: The most complete version is an English manuscript
points.body: The Song of Roland is a French epic that took shape around the 12th century, belonging to the genre of Chanson de Geste (songs of deeds), and it spread with 12th-century French cultural hegemony to regions including Britain. But its most complete and oldest surviving version is not from France proper — it is an English manuscript, catalogued as Oxford Digby 23. This manuscript was at some point sewn together with a completely unrelated book by a later hand, which is why it is called Digby 23 B, and A is that "other book." Who sewed them together is unknown; possibly some monk felt both were his favourite books.

points.h: Every stanza is a camera position
points.body: The poem is organised in laisses (stanzas) of varying length, and each laisse is like a camera focus: when the scene or the mood changes, you change laisse. The whole poem is in decasyllabic meter, cut in performance into four plus six: the first four syllables rise, then a dramatic pause, then the last six syllables fall, overall close to iambic turning into trochaic. Recited over and over this becomes hypnotic, and the poem runs four thousand lines — hours of recitation.

points.h: At peak emotion, the same action is performed three times
points.body: This kind of epic has a convention that is very hard for a reteller to handle: when the action is especially intense or the emotion especially strong, it will use several consecutive laisses to tell the same action from three angles, a kind of slow motion in verse. For example, Roland's refusal to blow the oliphant is told three times, with almost no gap between them. This is also why it reads like an action film or a comic: scenes cut hard, with no softening transition — for instance, "Roland dies, his soul ascends to heaven" is followed directly by "the Emperor arrives at Roncevaux."

points.h: The end of the manuscript preserves the performer's name
points.body: Digby 23 is very likely a real minstrel's working copy. Line 4002 of the poem, its final line, says roughly: "here ends the song of deeds; Turoldus will tell no more." This line comes before Charlemagne's lament, so it reads more like the performer saying: this is too sad, I cannot go on. The name Turoldus does not appear in the poem, and he is not a known scribe, so scholars lean toward him being the owner of this manuscript, the performer of this performance.

points.h: Pocket-size dimensions give away that it was for work
points.body: The manuscript measures only about six and a half inches by four and a half inches, a pocket copy you could carry on your person, not a finely bound volume for a wealthy collector. It is itself heavily worn and not refined, and contains some small annotations of unclear meaning. Together these features point to a professional performer on the move: he might have travelled alone with an instrument, or been the lead singer or narrator of a troupe, with someone in front of him doing the physical performance. Such people were jongleurs — the source of the later word juggler.

points.h: The dialect pins this performer to England
points.body: The manuscript is not in the French of central France, nor continental French, but in Anglo-Norman, which suggests this performer was probably Anglo-Norman, performing in Britain or at least in Normandy. The dialect features are very specific: continental French O and OU are replaced by U, so Roland becomes Rulant, l'or becomes l'ur; Anglo-Norman French is also losing final soft e. These changes even begin to break the originally strict decasyllabic meter, leaving some lines with only nine syllables or swelling to eleven.

points.h: Accent drift alone can date a manuscript
points.body: Scholars' grasp of this dialect is fine enough that they can date the manuscript to between 1140 and 1170 based on the degree of accent drift. The method is similar to scholars reconstructing Shakespearean pronunciation, tracking regular changes in syllables and sounds. Poetry is especially suited to this kind of reconstruction, because meter and rhyme expose which sounds were dropped and which were added. For many jongleurs, French was a second language anyway, spoken with a dialect accent, and they spelled by sound.

points.h: A French epic, an English artifact
points.body: Although this is a French poem about an old French king, the manuscript is an English thing, performed for Britons at the time. There is no other equally complete manuscript to compare line by line, but there are abundant records of The Song of Roland being sung before and after this manuscript, and scholars can use them to judge where this performer departed from what the genre should look like. The episode goes on to cover the poem's symbolic system, how its audience was constructed, and what the music sounded like.
